Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/tables.Rmd
tables.Rmd

This page shows how to build a table, style it and render it for the output you need. phwstyle’s table builders count, group and total your records. Each one returns a data frame that remembers its layout, so you can render the same object in Word, HTML, Excel or a Shiny app. You can also style a table you built yourself, with dplyr or by hand.

All data on this page is made up.

Output Function
Word, PDF, PowerPoint phw_flextable()
HTML, Quarto phw_gt()
Interactive HTML, Shiny phw_reactable() and phw_datatable()
Excel phw_write_xlsx() 
library(phwstyle)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1)
dat <- tibble(
  group = sample(c("Group A", "Group B", "Group C"), 400, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.45, 0.4, 0.15)),
  type = factor(sample(c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3"), 400, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.45, 0.45, 0.1)),
                levels = c("Type 1", "Type 2", "Type 3")),
  year = sample(2024:2025, 400, replace = TRUE),
  quarter = sample(paste0("Q", 1:4), 400, replace = TRUE),
  days = rpois(400, 3)
)
col_labels <- list(group = "Group", type = "Type", year = "Year", quarter = "Quarter")

cases <- tibble(
  age_group = sample(c("0-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  sex = sample(c("Female", "Male"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  setting = sample(c("Setting 1", "Setting 2", "Setting 3"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  days = rpois(300, 4),
  outcome = sample(c("Outcome X", "Outcome Y"), 300, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2))
)

Summary tables

Characteristics by group

phw_summary_table() describes each variable in one table. Categories show a count and a percentage, and numbers show a median and interquartile range. Give by to split the columns by a group.

phw_summary_table(cases, by = outcome,
                  labels = list(age_group = "Age group", sex = "Sex", setting = "Setting",
                                days = "Days to recovery")) |>
  phw_flextable(caption = "Characteristics by outcome")

A table you built yourself

phw_as_summary() styles a table made elsewhere. Every row of a plain data frame looks the same to a renderer. Mark it as a summary table and the renderers show bold variable rows, indented levels and a bold total row.

Name the column that says what each row is with row_type. Its values are "variable", "level", "subtotal", "group" and "total". The column is not kept in the result. Add a footnote with note.

This example builds a table with dplyr. Each block is a heading row followed by its levels, and a total row closes the table.

block <- function(data, var, heading) {
  counts <- data |> count(level = .data[[var]], name = "cases")
  bind_rows(
    tibble(Characteristic = heading, Cases = NA, Percent = NA, kind = "variable"),
    counts |> transmute(Characteristic = level, Cases = cases,
                        Percent = round(100 * cases / sum(cases), 1), kind = "level")
  )
}

mine <- bind_rows(
  block(cases, "age_group", "Age group"),
  block(cases, "sex", "Sex"),
  tibble(Characteristic = "All cases", Cases = nrow(cases), Percent = 100, kind = "total")
) |>
  phw_as_summary(row_type = kind, note = "Example data. Percentages are of all cases.")

Printed, the table is still a data frame. The kind column has gone, and the row layout travels with the table.

mine
#>  Characteristic Cases Percent
#>       Age group    NA      NA
#>            0-14    72    24.0
#>           15-44    88    29.3
#>           45-64    66    22.0
#>             65+    74    24.7
#>             Sex    NA      NA
#>          Female   150    50.0
#>            Male   150    50.0
#>       All cases   300   100.0
#> Example data. Percentages are of all cases.

The same object works in every renderer.

phw_datatable() and phw_write_xlsx() read the same layout. See the Excel section to save it as a workbook.

Cross-tabulations

phw_crosstab() counts by two variables and adds totals. Set percent to "row", "column" or "total" to show percentages as well. phw_flextable_heat() then colours the counts.

Rates

phw_rate_table() takes aggregated counts and populations. It divides cases by population, multiplies by per (100,000 by default) and gives confidence limits for each rate. The limits come from the Poisson distribution, using the exact (Garwood) method. Each variable in groups becomes its own section, and total adds an overall row. See ?phw_rate_table for the details.

agg <- tidyr::expand_grid(sex = c("Female", "Male"), age_group = c("0-14", "15-44", "45-64", "65+")) |>
  mutate(cases = rpois(n(), c(10, 25, 35, 50)),
         population = round(runif(n(), 60, 140)) * 1000)
phw_rate_table(agg, c(age_group, sex), cases, population,
               labels = list(age_group = "Age group", sex = "Sex")) |>
  phw_flextable(caption = "Rate per 100,000 by age group and sex")

Confidence intervals use the exact Poisson method.

Use phw_poisson_ci() when you only need the limits for a vector of counts, for example to draw your own intervals. It returns a data frame with lower and upper, for the same calculation that phw_rate_table() uses. Change conf_level to change the level.

phw_poisson_ci(c(0, 5, 40))
#>       lower     upper
#> 1  0.000000  3.688879
#> 2  1.623486 11.668332
#> 3 28.576586 54.468647
phw_poisson_ci(c(0, 5, 40), conf_level = 0.99)
#>       lower     upper
#> 1  0.000000  5.298317
#> 2  1.077928 14.149759
#> 3 25.585966 59.363067

Risks by exposure

phw_risk_table() takes one row per person. For each level of each exposure, it gives the number of people, the number of cases and the attack rate, which is cases divided by people. It compares each level with the reference level, giving a relative risk with a confidence interval and a p-value from Fisher’s exact test. Set p_value = FALSE to leave the p-value out. See ?phw_risk_table for the details.

ob <- tibble(exposure_a = sample(c("Yes", "No"), 120, replace = TRUE),
             exposure_b = sample(c("Yes", "No"), 120, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(ill = rbinom(n(), 1, if_else(exposure_a == "Yes", 0.6, 0.15)))
phw_risk_table(ob, c(exposure_a, exposure_b), ill,
               labels = list(exposure_a = "Exposure A", exposure_b = "Exposure B")) |>
  phw_flextable(caption = "Attack rate and relative risk by exposure")

Nested groups

phw_group_table() nests row groups inside each other. Give the row groups outermost first. Each group row (Group A, B, C) shows the total for its group, the groups inside are indented, and the main groups are shaded and separated with space.

tab <- phw_group_table(dat, rows = c(group, type), cols = year, labels = col_labels)
phw_flextable(tab, caption = "Counts by group and type", source = "Example data")

Totals

totals takes any of "group" (totals on each group row), "subgroup" (a block with each type summed across all groups) and "table" (a grand total). total_position puts the table total at the top or bottom, and subtotal_position = "below" moves group totals to their own row.

phw_group_table(dat, c(group, type), labels = col_labels,
                totals = c("group", "subgroup", "table"),
                subtotal_position = "below", total_position = "top") |>
  phw_flextable()

Layout and percentages

layout = "columns" gives each level its own column, so the inner groups shift to the right. percent = "parent" shows each row as a share of the group above it. "column" and "row" are also available.

phw_group_table(dat, c(group, type), labels = col_labels, layout = "columns",
                percent = "parent", separate = "both") |>
  phw_flextable()

Nested columns

Columns can nest too, here quarters within years, with a total for each year and overall.

nested <- phw_group_table(dat, c(group, type), c(year, quarter), labels = col_labels,
                          col_totals = c("group", "table"))
phw_gt(nested, caption = "Counts by quarter")

Other statistics

By default rows are counted. Give value and fun for anything else. Group and total rows are calculated from their records, not by adding up rows.

phw_group_table(dat, c(group, type), year, value = days,
                fun = function(x) round(mean(x), 1), labels = col_labels) |>
  phw_flextable(caption = "Mean days")

Render the same table anywhere

flextable

phw_flextable() builds a flextable from a data frame or any table above. It adds the caption, the number formats and the source line. style chooses the look. The default is "booktabs", with horizontal rules only.

small <- tibble(Area = paste("Area", LETTERS[1:4]), Cases = c(120, 85, 64, 19),
                Rate = c(48.2, 39.5, 27.1, 12.9))
phw_flextable(small, caption = "booktabs", style = "booktabs")

Heat, bars and group colours

phw_flextable_heat() fills the cells of the columns you choose with a sequential palette. It picks white or dark text for each cell. Choose columns the way you do in dplyr, and use palette and domain to change the colours and the range they span.

phw_flextable(small) |>
  phw_flextable_heat(j = c(Cases, Rate), palette = "blues")

With palette = "rag", the cells are red, amber or green and a shape comes before each value, so the meaning survives black-and-white print. Give two cut points in breaks, and set higher_is_better = FALSE when a low value is good. "rag_accessible" uses navy in place of green.

phw_flextable(small) |>
  phw_flextable_heat(j = Rate, palette = "rag", breaks = c(20, 40))

phw_flextable_groups() colours cells by the group they contain, using the colours of your charts. Give a colour key with key and the group keeps its colour across tables and charts (see colour keys). Set what = "text" to colour the text, and rows = TRUE to colour the whole row.

by_group <- tibble(Group = c("Group A", "Group B", "Group C", "Unknown"),
                   Cases = c(120, 85, 64, 9))
phw_flextable(by_group) |>
  phw_flextable_groups(Group)

A flextable you made yourself

phw_flextable_theme() styles a flextable you built with the flextable package. It takes the same style choices.

flextable::flextable(head(small, 3)) |>
  phw_flextable_theme(style = "zebra")

use_phw_flextable() sets the defaults for every new flextable in your session, so put it in a setup chunk. It returns your earlier defaults, so you can put them back.

old <- use_phw_flextable()
flextable::flextable(head(small, 3))

do.call(flextable::set_flextable_defaults, old)

gt

phw_gt() builds a gt table with the same caption, number formats and source line. It understands summary tables and group tables.

phw_gt(small, caption = "Cases by area", source = "Example data")
Cases by area
Area Cases Rate
Area A 120 48.2
Area B 85 39.5
Area C 64 27.1
Area D 19 12.9
Source: Example data

phw_gt_theme() styles a gt table you built yourself. Set stripe = TRUE to shade alternate rows.

gt::gt(small) |>
  gt::tab_header(title = "Cases by area") |>
  phw_gt_theme(stripe = TRUE)
Cases by area
Area Cases Rate
Area A 120 48.2
Area B 85 39.5
Area C 64 27.1
Area D 19 12.9

gtsummary

use_phw_gtsummary() sets a theme, so every gtsummary table is styled when printed with gt or converted with as_flex_table().

use_phw_gtsummary()

Interactive tables and Excel

phw_reactable() and phw_datatable() make tables you can sort and search. See reactable. phw_write_xlsx() saves any of these tables as a workbook. See Excel.

For finished examples of every table, see the gallery.
